articles.title: There was little fuss about data centers in the last election. Now they could sway the midterms.
articles.summary: AI data centers have become a key issue in the 2026 midterms.
articles.body:
Opposition to data centers, an issue barely on anyone's radar in the 2024 election, has now united voters across the political spectrum .

According to a May Gallup poll , more than 70% of Americans are opposed to AI data center construction in their local area. It makes sense when you consider that this midterms cycle is heavily focused on rising living costs . Data centers — facilities that store, process and distribute digital data, and have become more common in the AI era — use up massive amounts of water and electricity, raising concerns that the costs will be passed down to local communities in the form of electric bill hikes and water rate increases.

The Data Center Opposition Project , which tracks the rise of grassroots nonprofits in the U.S. that are against the development of data centers, recently found that more than 200 new groups popped up between June and August of this year, suggesting the issue has salience with voters across the country.

Heading into the midterms, that could be a major problem for candidates and incumbents who have supported data center projects. And in many cases, their opponents are making sure voters are well aware of their positions.

President Trump has strongly supported data centers. He views them as key to winning the AI race against China, but also for economic growth and the creation of local jobs. "If they want to be successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place, let Data Reign," he wrote in an August Truth Social post. On the flip side, progressives like Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Sen. Bernie Sanders have proposed a national moratorium on new AI data centers "until strong national safeguards are in place."

Ohio will soon be home to what the Trump administration calls the " world's largest AI data center. " SB Energy , a development company, will build and own the site, with OpenAI leasing it for 20 years. Nvidia announced a $1.5 billion investment in SB Energy as part of the deal. The PORTS-Pike Technology Campus , as the Ohio data center project is known, is slated to begin construction this year. And like many data centers, it's in a rural area near Piketon, a village of roughly 2,200 residents about 70 miles south of Columbus, where there is ample space for the sprawling facility.

Residents there have mixed feelings about the project. Some are being offered significant sums of money for their properties, which may mean a piece of land that's been in their family for generations. Samantha McCaughey, a barista at the Village Brew Coffee House in Piketon, told Yahoo that her grandfather is weighing a six-figure offer for the family's nearly 100-acre property near the data center site.

"They've lived there their whole life, so it's really difficult for them," McCaughey said. "They're still kind of on the fence, but I mean, with everything going on, is it worth even staying if everything is changing?"

In June, a citizen-led effort to put a statewide data center ban on the November ballot fell short . However, 18 communities in Ohio will have data center measures on their local ballots this year. Half of the petitions ask voters to decide whether to ban any centers that draw more than 25 megawatts of energy from the local grid per month. And there are more than 100 moratoriums on new data centers in communities across the state. An August poll from Bowling Green State University found 78% of Ohioans support these temporary moratoriums.

Ohio ranks fourth among states with the most operational data centers, and the issue has been a centerpiece of former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown's ad campaign against incumbent Republican Sen. Jon Husted. An AdImpact analysis of spending on campaign ads this cycle found Democrats far outspent Republicans on data center-themed ads, with most of them either attacking the centers or linking a candidate to the center's potential negative impacts. Brown's campaign spent $2.4 million on data center-themed ads. Those included attacks on Husted for his past support of data centers, repeating the label given to him as "the face of data centers in Ohio." In recent months, however, Husted has worked to put guardrails on them.

"They're devouring our farmland, sucking up our water, and using our energy," Brown says in one ad , where he accuses Husted of giving huge tax breaks to companies like Meta, which is building a 715,000-square-foot data center in northwest Ohio. "I'm fighting to give you a voice to make sure these data centers don't flood our communities and raise our electric rates."

And indeed, the water and electricity-guzzling facilities are needed to power artificial intelligence. According to a 2025 report from the International Energy Agency , the typical AI data center consumes as much electricity as 100,000 households every year. The agency predicts the largest data centers under construction will use 20 times that amount.

The facilities also consume vast amounts of water, in part because they need to cool their processor chips. According to the Environmental and Energy Study Institute , large data centers may use up to five million gallons of water per day. A Bloomberg analysis found that in areas with "significant data center activity," wholesale electricity prices rose as much as 267% from 2020 to 2025. Those costs are being passed along to utility customers.

Axios reported in August that an internal memo from the National Republican Senatorial Committee said strong opposition to data centers had become damaging to Husted's reelection bid. In addition, the race may be a warning signal for other candidates. "If [Husted] loses and data centers get the blame, politicians across the country will take notice — and they will not go near the next one," the memo says. "This has become a sleeper issue for the entire election cycle."

Recent polling averages show Brown leading Husted by around 3 percentage points and the nonpartisan Cook Political Report has rated the race as a toss up .

Husted's campaign secretary, Tom Evans, noted in an email to Yahoo that Husted had introduced the Senate companion bill to the Ratepayer Protection Act (RPA), which passed the U.S. House on Sept. 16 by a vote of 417-3. The RPA would require state utility regulators to consider adopting a federal standard under which large data centers would cover the extra costs of upgrades — potentially preventing those costs from getting passed along to other customers.

A vote on Husted's bill was blocked by Senate Democrats, who said it didn't go far enough. "Sherrod Brown and his friends would rather play politics and stick Ohio families with higher electric bills than pass a commonsense solution," Evans said to Yahoo, pointing to Brown's earlier support of a data center project in 2015.

While some Ohio communities have pushed back hard against new data centers, in Piketon, locals still seem uncertain.

"Residents have been asking good questions — hard questions — about data centers and we are asking good, hard questions too," Pike County Commissioner Tony Montgomery told Yahoo. "We have set no deadline on considering this project and have involved public officials throughout the county in our review."

McCaughey said she likes Piketon's "cozy" vibe and is a little wary of the coming growth, but that she sees the upside as well. "It's cool seeing how things are going to grow and how many people are going to have jobs that might otherwise have been struggling," she said.

Local officials say they expect an estimated 35,000 temporary construction jobs and 2,500 permanent jobs to be created. Meanwhile, data center operators argue that when one of them enters a community, other businesses, including tech companies, financial institutions and retail companies, usually follow.

Brown told Yahoo that local governments shouldn't offer tax breaks as incentives for developers to build data centers in their communities. "They're billionaires. They don't need tax breaks to come in," he said, adding that local residents should have a say in decisions about data center proposals. "Local communities have just been run over in this."

He added that local communities should make sure any agreements require data centers to pay for their own power usage.

When asked about rural landowners near data centers who are debating whether to sell or stay, Brown advised those who decide to sell to "make sure they drive a hard bargain, and that [the data centers] are responsible with the land."

Data centers take center stage in the midterms

Ohio isn't the only state where data centers have become a political issue — and Brown isn't the only candidate spotlighting his opponent's support for them in the midterms races.

Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, who is running for the Senate in Michigan, has criticized his Republican opponent Mike Rogers for his investments in companies tied to data centers (the sound of a data center is all you hear in one of El-Sayed's campaign ads). In August, Rogers called for a one-year moratorium on new data center development. Meanwhile, officials in Wayne County, which includes Detroit, recently voted to advance a proposed 1.5 million-square-foot Google data center.

In Florida, which ranks 12th among the states with the most data centers currently operating or planned, Democrat David Jolly and Republican Byron Donalds have both run ads on the issue in the gubernatorial race. Jolly has called for a moratorium and criticizes Donalds for receiving donations from AI and data center companies . Donalds has called for companies building the data centers to absorb their costs.

This is an idea that continues to gain traction even among those who support data center construction.

On Wednesday, Trump posted on Truth Social that he had " come to a very strong conclusion " — that new and large data centers should "make their own electricity, and give or sell excess back to the local community, or grid" if companies want to make them popular. The comment signals how prominent the issue has become for voters.

Some candidates have been hearing more from constituents concerned about proposed projects as they meet face-to-face. At a town hall in his southwestern Pennsylvania district on Oct. 17, Rep. Chris Deluzio said communities should have a voice in decisions related to data centers.

"I don't think you should get steamrolled by these corporations," Deluzio said. "There's a lot of money in this industry. I don't think they need our public money."

Governors in some states that welcomed data centers have recently pumped the brakes in response to the public backlash. Gov. Josh Shapiro of Pennsylvania signed an executive order in August tightening permitting requirements for large data centers. The order requires local approval before certain new projects can receive state permits, and removes existing projects from the state's fast-tracked permitting process. That provision applies to a $20 billion commitment Amazon made last year to build multiple AI data centers across the state, which Shapiro embraced at the time.

And in Virginia — a state whose northern region has become known as Data Center Alley — Gov. Abigail Spanberger presented a set of legislative proposals that would curb data center development. Her "Data Center Accountability Framework" stops short of a statewide moratorium, but includes plans to lower energy costs, promote clean energy and put environmental protections in place. It would also bar non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) between local governments and data center developers. Many argue NDAs prevent residents from learning details of data center proposals until late in the process.

NDAs have been used in data center projects across Virginia, researchers at the University of Mary Washington found. And Virginia has had data centers long before the facilities became associated with AI. In 1998, two years after AOL moved into Loudoun County , Va., Equinix built the region's first data center partly to help store the internet service provider's data. Amazon built its first data center in Loudoun in 2006.

According to the county's website , Loudoun boasts "the highest concentration of data centers anywhere in the world." In fiscal year 2026, its data centers brought in $1.2 billion in property tax revenue, it says. That number is projected to climb to $1.3 billion, or 40% of the county's overall budget, in 2027.

With the midterms looming, an October New York Times/Siena University poll found that while data centers are not the top issue for most Ohio voters, it's a bigger midterm issue there than in four other states — Alaska, Iowa, Kansas and Texas — that were surveyed. Most Ohio voters are opposed to new data center construction, and more of them said they trusted Brown to handle the issue over Husted.

For her part, McCaughey said her family is accustomed to living in a rural area, and she doesn't want to see that go away. "My dad loves going out and hunting and just being in the woods," she said. "Knowing that it would be lost is really sad."

articles.title: Isofix: O que é e como usar para transporte infantil seguro | G1
articles.standfirst: O Isofix é a melhor e mais segura forma para transportar uma criança pequena no veículo de passeio; veja como garantir a instalação segura, segundo as regras do Contran.
articles.summary: Entenda o que é Isofix, sistema mais seguro para transportar crianças no carro. Veja como garantir a instalação correta, conforme as regras do Contran, e evite erros.
articles.body:
Pontos de ancoragem do Isofix em um Volkswagen Golf — Foto: divulgação/Volkswagen

A escolha e o uso adequado da cadeirinha infantil ainda despertam dúvidas entre pais e responsáveis, mesmo após a sua obrigatoriedade em veículos de passeio, estabelecida em setembro de 2010.

Uma das formas de prender o bebê conforto, cadeirinha ou assento de elevação nos carros é o Isofix, que ancora a cadeirinha ao assento traseiro do carro. Porém, a lei do Isofix foi sancionada em 2015 e somente em 2020 é que passou a ser obrigatória para todos os veículos novos fabricados ou importados no país.

Este tipo de ancoragem exige pontos de fixação específicos, tanto no veículo quanto na cadeirinha.

O sistema é composto por dois pontos de fixação na base da cadeirinha ou do bebê-conforto, que se encaixam a dois pontos no veículo, localizados no vão entre o assento e o encosto do banco traseiro.

Localizar os pontos de ancoragem no banco traseiro , que podem ser visíveis como na imagem acima, ou escondidos. Neste caso, um ícone de cadeirinha infantil ou o nome "Isofix" fica visível.

Guiar os pontos da cadeirinha aos locais do banco e empurrar , até escutar um "clique".

Em algumas cadeirinhas, uma indicação em verde aparece próxima do local de ancoragem no assento do veículo.

Ponto de ancoragem Isofix em um Volkswagen Golf — Foto: divulgação/Volkswagen

Um terceiro ponto pode estar no carro e ele se liga a uma espécie de gancho da cadeirinha, evitando que o dispositivo se movimente. Esse ponto tem nome de Top Tether e, se estiver no seu carro, estará em um dos seguintes locais:

Na parte de trás do encosto (na área do porta-malas, como na imagem abaixo);

Na lateral do carro (na mesma área de onde saem os cintos de segurança).

Top tether em um Volvo XC40 — Foto: divulgação/Volvo

Bebê conforto, cadeirinha e assento com elevação: os dispositivos indispensáveis para transportar crianças — Foto: g1

Confira abaixo as principais dúvidas sobre transporte seguro de crianças em carros:

Como usar e fixar o assento de elevação?

Quando a criança pode ir no banco da frente?

No papel, a regra do Conselho Nacional de Trânsito (Contran) define faixas etárias para cada tipo de equipamento:

Cadeirinha: de 1 a 4 anos ou entre 9 kg e 18 kg;

Assento de elevação: de 4 a 7 anos; entre 15 kg e 36 kg ou até 1,45 m de altura;

Banco traseiro com cinto de segurança: de 7 anos a 10 anos, desde que a criança tenha pelo menos 1,45 m de altura.

O uso incorreto da cadeirinha, além da insegurança para o bebê ou a criança, inclui multa de R$ 293,47, sete pontos na CNH e retenção do veículo.

O Inmetro, que certifica os produtos, classifica os dispositivos por grupos que combinam idade, peso e altura. Há modelos que abrangem mais de um grupo e podem ser usados por mais tempo.

“Existem cadeirinhas certificadas que comportam de 0 kg a 25 kg, por exemplo. Outras duram praticamente todo o tempo em que a criança vai precisar usar dispositivo de retenção”, explica Gustavo Kuster, do Inmetro.

O modelo da cadeirinha deve acompanhar o crescimento da criança, garantindo que ela esteja sempre firme e protegida. Como cada versão é indicada para uma faixa etária específica, a troca do equipamento se torna necessária conforme o desenvolvimento.

A transição entre os dispositivos deve considerar, na seguinte ordem de prioridade:

Um bebê que já não cabe no bebê conforto, por exemplo, pode ir para a cadeirinha, mesmo que ainda não tenha completado a idade mínima para a transição.

“Se ela ainda cabe naquele dispositivo, está confortável, com o cinto bem preso, pode continuar nele”, afirma Kuster.

A posição do bebê conforto — voltado para o encosto do banco — é recomendada por causa da anatomia dos recém-nascidos. “O bebê nasce com a cabeça maior que o corpo, como na forma de um martelo. Nessa posição, ele fica mais protegido”, explica Celso Arruda, especialista da Unicamp.

Para os mais crescidos, a altura é o fator mais importante na hora de dispensar o assento de elevação.

Crianças com menos de 1,45 m não devem usar apenas o cinto de segurança, mesmo que tenham mais de 7 anos. O assento serve para posicionar corretamente o cinto de três pontos, que deve passar pelo peito.

“Se ela ainda não tiver altura suficiente e quiser continuar usando inclusive a cadeirinha completa, sem dispensar o encosto, ainda que tenha mais de 4 anos ou mais de 36 kg, tudo bem. Desde que esteja confortável”, afirma Kuster.

O lugar mais seguro para transportar a criança é o banco traseiro, com cinto de três pontos e o dispositivo adequado. Mas há exceções.

Em carros que só têm cinto de dois pontos no banco de trás — e não há cadeirinha certificada para esse tipo de cinto — o ideal é levar a criança no banco da frente, com cinto de três pontos e o equipamento de retenção.

Mas é preciso desligar o airbag, nos carros equipados com o dispositivo e a depender da posição, para não eclodir em caso de acidente e causar mais danos do que proteger a criança.

“Dar um jeito de fixar a cadeirinha feita para cinto de três pontos em um cinto com dois pontos é ruim”, alerta Fábio Viviani, especialista em segurança veicular.

“Pode até parecer que ficou firme, mas nos crash tests é impressionante ver as forças envolvidas. A cadeirinha sem esse terceiro ponto de fixação não vai trabalhar da maneira como foi projetada”.

Nesses casos, a recomendação é recuar o banco dianteiro ao máximo, para afastar a criança do painel.

O Contran permite o transporte no banco da frente em situações específicas:

Crianças a partir de 10 anos, com cinto de segurança;

Quando o banco traseiro só tem cinto de dois pontos;

Em veículos sem banco traseiro, como picapes de cabine simples;

Quando há mais crianças do que lugares no banco traseiro — a de maior estatura pode ir na frente;

Segundo a Senatran, apenas bebê conforto, cadeirinha e assento de elevação são considerados dispositivos adequados. O Inmetro reforça que não há certificação para outros tipos de equipamentos.

“Sem um equipamento certificado, ou seja, que passou por testes rigorosos, a criança não estará devidamente protegida”, afirma Viviani.

articles.title: Man caught in car with £14k of drugs as a lamb ate chips in the back seat avoids jail
articles.summary: Police officers found the animal in the back seat of John McNeil's car on the M74 in Glasgow.
articles.body:
A man who was caught in a car with £14,000 of drugs, while a lamb ate from a bag of chips in the back seat, has avoided jail.

John McNeil, 56, was a passenger in Lindsey Sangster's vehicle which was stopped by police on the M74 in Glasgow on 22 April 2023.

Bags of heroin and cocaine were later recovered by a police dog underneath the front passenger seat of the Volkswagen Golf.

When quizzed about the animal - called Pablo - a sergeant claimed Sangster's partner McNeil told him she was a "trainee shepherdess." The duo were found guilty in September of possession of cocaine and diamorphine with intent to supply.

The pair claimed they had tried to save the lamb - named after Colombian drug lord Pablo Escobar - from a "dangerous position" on the middle of the road.

The court previously heard Pablo belonged to North Lanrigg Farm in Motherwell, which is owned by farmer Kirsty Mair.

A joint minute of agreed evidence said Mair had not given them permission to have the lamb.

Sgt Nick Twigg, 42, told jurors that he had reason to stop Sangster's car on the motorway, with Sangster, McNeil and another man in the vehicle.

An initial search found a glass pipe in the driver's door pocket while others were seized from McNeil and the man.

He said: "I asked Sangster where it [the lamb] came from and McNeil said that she was a trainee shepherdess."

Prosecutor Julianna Keenan asked the officer if there was evidence of this and he replied: "No, the lamb at the time was eating a bag of chips left on the back seat. There were no bottles."

More stories from Glasgow & West Scotland

A police dog named Billy later found £4,640 of cocaine and £10,050 of heroin under the front passenger seat within two bags.

The purity of the cocaine was stated to be no less than 76%.

In a joint minute of agreed evidence, Keenan said: "Officers were of the opinion that the circumstances of this case indicate the supply of cocaine and heroin due to the amount recovered being excessive for personal use."

Pablo was taken to a farm in Ayrshire where it was held for 48 to 72 hours before being returned to Mair.

A charge of resetting the lamb was dropped by the Crown mid-trial as there was "no reported theft" at the time.

McNeil told jurors in his evidence that he had experience with animals, having worked in the past with his father, who is a retired agricultural contractor.

He stated they came across Pablo on the middle of the road on the way home to Ayrshire after a journey to Edinburgh for the other man to purchase a car.

McNeil claimed that Pablo was "dehydrated" and appeared not have been fed for a couple of hours.

He told the court that the plan was to "take him back to the owner" as Pablo had identity markings on his ears.

McNeil denied any knowledge of the drugs in the car, as did Sangster.

Jurors were told that Sangster was under the influence of drugs at the time when she was behind the wheel and pleaded guilty at separate proceedings.

She was disqualified from driving for 18 months and ordered to do 100 hours of unpaid work.

Bronwyn Moore, defending McNeil at the sentencing, said her client was now a team leader at a construction company and that he was "at the height of his addiction" when arrested.

McNeil, of Fairlie, North Ayrshire, was back in the dock to be sentenced while Sangster, of Kilbirnie, did not appear and a warrant was granted for her arrest.

Sheriff Tony Kelly ordered McNeil to do 300 hours of unpaid work and tagged him for six months, meaning he must stay indoors between 20:00 and 05:00.

The sheriff said he had been advised the risk of McNeil offending again was low.

After the lamb was returned to Mair, she said he was in fine health and happy with "his new pet lamb pals".

articles.title: Delhi records season’s first ‘very poor’ AQI at 324; GRAP-2 curbs imposed, border checks snarl traffic
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Delhi’s air quality deteriorated to the ‘very poor’ category for the first time this season on Monday, with the Air Quality Index (AQI)
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Delhi’s air quality deteriorated to the ‘very poor’ category for the first time this season on Monday, with the Air Quality Index (AQI) settling at 324 by 4 pm, the highest level in nine months.As pollution levels worsened, the Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM) invoked Stage 2 of the Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP) across Delhi-NCR, while intensified checks at the capital’s borders to enforce vehicle restrictions left commuters stuck in long traffic queues.The AQI of 324 was the highest recorded since February 4, when it stood at 339. The city’s pollution levels had risen sharply over the previous two days, from 117 in the ‘moderate’ category on October 31 to 261 in the ‘poor’ category on November 1, before entering the ‘very poor’ category on Monday.Three of Delhi’s air quality monitoring stations reported ‘severe’ pollution at 4pm. Jahangirpuri recorded the worst AQI at 436, followed by Rohini at 415 and Punjabi Bagh at 413.Of the city’s 58 monitoring stations, 37 reported ‘very poor’ air quality, 17 were in the ‘poor’ category and one recorded ‘moderate’ air quality.Fine particulate matter, or PM2.5, remained the dominant pollutant. These particles, measuring 2.5 micrometres or less, can penetrate deep into the lungs and enter the bloodstream.GRAP Stage 2 invoked across Delhi-NCRThe CAQM said Delhi’s AQI had risen sharply due to unfavourable meteorological conditions and was likely to remain in the ‘very poor’ category over the coming days, according to forecasts by the India Meteorological Department and the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology.Stage 2 of GRAP applies when the AQI is between 301 and 400. The emergency measures are intended to prevent further deterioration in air quality.The AQI is expected to remain in the ‘very poor’ category from November 3 to 5, according to the Air Quality Early Warning System for Delhi, before improving marginally to the ‘poor’ category over the subsequent six days.The Decision Support System for Delhi estimated that the transport sector contributed 19.2% to the city’s pollution on Monday.Industries in Delhi and peripheral areas accounted for 4.2%, while residential activities contributed 4.9%. Stubble burning accounted for 8.4% of the pollution, with other sources contributing 20.7%.Among neighbouring NCR districts, Jhajjar accounted for 6.9% of the pollution, followed by Sonipat at 5.1%, Gurgaon at 2.9%, Rohtak at 2.7%, Ghaziabad at 2.6%, Baghpat at 2.4%, and Panipat and Bhiwani at 2% each. Gautam Buddha Nagar accounted for 1.9%.Border checks leave commuters stuck for hoursThe second day of the restrictions on vehicles entering Delhi saw intensified checks at several interstate borders, triggering long traffic queues on roads connecting the capital with Haryana and Uttar Pradesh.Heavy congestion was reported at the Delhi-Gurgaon, Delhi-Noida, Delhi-Ghaziabad, Delhi-Sonipat and Delhi-Najafgarh borders. On NH-48, traffic remained backed up for several kilometres near the Sirhaul toll plaza, affecting both the main carriageway and service roads. Similar snarls were reported near Noida and Ghaziabad.At the Aya Nagar border, Delhi Traffic Police and Transport Department teams turned back vehicles that did not meet the prescribed BS-VI emission standards.Officials said checks were being conducted across borders under different traffic police ranges, with fines also being issued for violations and incomplete vehicle documents.The restrictions, effective from November 1 as part of the winter pollution-control measures, bar petrol and diesel vehicles registered outside Delhi that do not meet BS-VI emission standards from entering the capital. Electric and CNG vehicles, along with BS-VI-compliant vehicles, are exempt.The enforcement is being jointly carried out by the Delhi Environment and Transport Departments and the traffic police at several entry points, including Rajokri on NH-48, DND Flyway, Ghazipur, Singhu, Tikri and Badarpur.The Northern Range of Delhi Traffic Police said its teams checked 7,657 vehicles between midnight on November 1 and noon on November 2, turning back 609 vehicles that did not comply with the restrictions.The drive was aimed at enforcing GRAP-related vehicle curbs and preventing non-compliant vehicles from entering the capital.On November 1, Delhi Traffic Police had checked 7,279 vehicles between midnight and 8 pm, turned back 714 and impounded 38, according to an earlier statement.The department also held a coordination meeting with police officials from neighbouring districts and used information boards, pamphlets, print media, social media and radio to publicise the restrictions.Delhi environment minister Manjinder Singh Sirsa said enforcement teams had checked 14,930 vehicles on November 1, issued 566 challans for Pollution Under Control Certificate violations and inspected 300 construction sites.HC declines interim relief against vehicle restrictionsThe Delhi high court on Monday refused to stay the ban on the entry of non-Delhi-registered vehicles that do not meet BS-VI emission standards. The restrictions are in force from November 1 to January 31.A bench of acting chief justice Nitin Wasudeo Sambre and justice Sanjay Sharma issued notice on a petition filed by Faridabad-based lawyer Gurmukh Dass Kohli and listed it for hearing with a related matter on November 27.The petitioner challenged the June 23 notification issued by the Department of Environment and Forests, arguing that the restriction discriminates between vehicles based on where they are registered rather than their emission standards.The plea pointed out that pre-BS-VI vehicles registered in Delhi remain allowed to ply in the capital, while comparable vehicles registered in Haryana are barred.The petition also argued that the blanket restriction applies irrespective of the AQI on a given day and affects the movement of residents across the integrated National Capital Region. It questioned the scientific basis of the decision and contended that less restrictive measures could have been considered.SC allows certified green crackers for two daysIn a separate development, the Supreme Court allowed the sale of certified green firecrackers in Delhi-NCR from November 4 to 6 and their bursting between 6am and 7am and 8pm and 10pm on November 7 and 8. The complete ban on firecrackers will be restored from November 9.The bench of justices MM Sundresh and Prasanna B Varale imposed conditions to prevent conventional and unauthorised firecrackers from being sold as green crackers.Manufacturers must have valid CSIR-NEERI certification and PESO licences, while each box must carry a product- and batch-specific QR code.Firecrackers containing barium, those not approved by CSIR-NEERI and crackers joined in series, commonly known as ‘ladis’, have been prohibited.The court also directed authorities to designate specific sale locations, with online sales prohibited, and asked police teams to inspect markets, verify QR codes and confiscate illegal firecrackers.No firecrackers will be allowed within 300 metres of hospitals, healthcare centres, old-age homes, educational institutions and notified silence zones.In its October 29 order, the court said a complete ban was facilitating the illegal sale of conventional firecrackers while preventing people from buying legitimate green crackers tested at established facilities.It also flagged the lack of adequate data on whether the ban imposed in 2024 had served its purpose, particularly in the absence of a significant improvement in AQI readings.The bench directed the CPCB, in consultation with state pollution control boards, to prepare daily air quality reports for the pre-Diwali period, November 2 to 6, Diwali, November 7 and 8, and the post-Diwali period, November 9 to 30.Authorities have also been asked to monitor pollution levels, inspect non-functional AQI monitoring stations and ensure post-festival waste clearance.The court warned that contempt action could be taken against officials for failing to implement its directions.(With agency inputs)You Can articles.title: Labour to end power-sharing with Greens in 11 councils over Zionism row
articles.summary: Labour's ruling National Executive Committee sets out where it is cutting ties with the Greens.
articles.body:
The Labour Party has pulled out of power-sharing agreements with the Green Party in 11 local councils, after the national party adopted a policy defining Zionism as a form of racism.

Labour councillors will no longer be in coalition with the Greens in areas including Sheffield, Warwick and Lewes.

Labour Party chair Bridget Phillipson said: "Labour has been clear from the start that the "Zionism is Racism" policy crosses a line and we cannot work with any party that supports it – at any level of government."

The Green Party said it was "hugely disappointed" that Labour had forced local leaders into "jeopardising successful progressive partnerships that are delivering benefits for residents".

In a joint statement, the Green Party and the Local Government Association Green Group said "top-down directives to break up and disrupt locally-run services are not in the interests of the residents we represent.

"We trust local communities, local councillors and local leaders to know what is best for them. We ask that others do the same."

In October, Green Party members backed a motion, entitled "Zionism is racism", which said Zionism was an ideology that supported an "ethnonationalist Jewish State in historic Palestine". It also backed a "single democratic Palestinian State", including in modern-day Israel.

Having been backed by party members, the motion became Green Party policy, but it has left senior figures bitterly divided . Jewish groups and opposition political parties have condemned it.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham told MPs in October that Labour would not partner with the Greens over the "antisemitic" policy.

Labour then issued an ultimatum from Labour's head office to Labour-Green councils, demanding that local Greens disown the motion passed by members at their national party conference.

Green groups were also asked to call on their party's national leadership to reconsider the policy.

Labour said there were local agreements in place in 18 authorities. Of those, Labour said 11 had not met the criteria it demanded.

Lewes District Council (The Green Party announced last week it was "mutually" ending its alliance with Labour)

Runnymede Borough Council (Labour says local co-operation had already ceased)

Labour said its conditions had been met in Broadland, Monmouthshire, North Somerset, Rother, West Oxfordshire and West Sussex. The party said that Coventry City Council does not have a formal arrangement in place and that no such deal will be made in the future.

It will continue co-operating with the Greens in the West of England mayoralty, where the deputy mayor is a Green member.

Green Party leader Zack Polanski has said the motion was "imperfect" but has defended its central premise , arguing that Israel's actions towards the Palestinian people are "clearly underpinned by racist ideology".

The collapse of co-operation at the local level could impact hundreds of thousands of residents through budgets and policy decisions taking longer to get voted through.

Green and Labour councillors in the impacted areas will now have to seek alternative coalition partners or try to govern as a minority administration.

One of the biggest councils to be affected is Sheffield, where 25 Labour councillors formed a power-sharing agreement with 20 Green councillors after the May 2026 elections for the Yorkshire city's 550,000 residents.

Responding to Labour's ultimatum, leader of the Sheffield Greens Angela Argenzio did not mention the motion in a letter but insisted local Green councillors "are not antisemitic".

Argenzio told local Labour representatives they were being "directed by your national party leader" rather than local concerns.

In a statement on Monday, the council's Labour leader Cllr Fran Belbin said her party would propose on Wednesday that it proceeds as a Labour minority administration.

"We now feel we are at the end of the road with the joint administration," she said.

"Our trust in Sheffield Greens is completely broken," she added, accusing them of a "refusal to stand up for Jewish citizens".

Green Party co-leader Rachel Millward, also the leader of Wealden Council, said: "It is ironic that a Labour prime minister who made a promise to solve problems, not score points, has now shown he is willing to disrupt well-run councils for fear of Green success."

She added: "It is utterly irresponsible to conflate criticism of the actions of the state of Israel with antisemitism. Many Jewish people strongly reject the illegal actions of the current Israeli government."

In Warwick, the local Green party said: "We refuse to condemn a democratically decided policy because of political intimidation."

It urged Prime Minister Andy Burnham to "reflect his own words in his actions and allow local Labour groups to decide for themselves".

Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme, Green group leader in Havant Netty Shepherd accused Labour of "performative politics" and said the end of their coalition would be a "complete disaster for residents".

"I am a local government councillor, I worry about people's bins, I worry about generating town centres - foreign policy is nothing to do with my remit," she added.

articles.title: Justin Thomas’ home life in 2026: Inside his $13.5 million Florida waterfront mansion, family routine, personal interests and relaxed lifestyle away from the PGA Tour spotlight
articles.summary: Discover the luxurious lifestyle of golfer Justin Thomas in his $13.5 million Florida waterfront mansion, where family, fashion, and relaxation take center stage away from the PGA Tour.
articles.body: Justin Thomas spends a good part of the year on the road, between tournaments, practice schedules and the routines of an elite golfer. Off the course, however, he lives a much more relaxed lifestyle, where family and the location of his Florida home on the water are priorities.That preference is reflected in the golfer’s reported $13.5 million Jupiter-Tequesta area home. The estate has river frontage, a private dock and is close to South Florida’s golf facilities, allowing for the balance between professional preparation and personal downtime.Inside Justin Thomas’ Florida waterfront mansionThe waterfront estate was reportedly bought by Justin Thomas in 2022 for about $13.5 million, up from his previous Jupiter home, which was valued at around $3.1 million. In the Tequesta-Jupiter area of South Florida, the mansion is more defined by water and privacy than a traditional golf community.The reported 7,600-square-foot property is located on the Loxahatchee River and features approximately 100 feet of riverfront and a private boat dock. These features allow Thomas to enjoy boating and the surrounding waterfront environment when he is not preparing for tournaments.Why does Justin Thomas prefer a waterfront property?Thomas’ selection suits his wish to get away from the pressures of professional golf and be somewhere peaceful. Competing on the PGA Tour for more than 30 weeks a year means a lot of his professional life revolves around golf courses, practice facilities and tournament schedules.At home, the river setting is a different atmosphere. There are chances to spend time on the water instead of golf at the private dock and in the outdoor surroundings.The property also provides easy access to elite golf facilities such as The Bear's Club in Jupiter. This means Thomas can continue his professional training without turning his home life into a sports environment entirely.How Justin Thomas balances golf and family lifeFamily life is an important part of Thomas' routine outside of tournaments. He is married to Jillian Thomas and they have a daughter, Molly Grace. They also have their dog Franklin in their home.Apparently, Thomas prefers a more relaxed routine during his breaks, compared to the tightly managed schedule he follows during tournament weeks. “College football, family time and the simple pleasures of home life are a contrast to the pressure of professional competition.”His life has taken on another dimension with his transition into fatherhood. Family commitments provide him with a chance to take a step back from the constant demands of travel, training and performance expectations.What Justin Thomas enjoys away from golfThomas is a passionate fan of fashion, particularly sneakers and footwear. He reportedly has a collection of popular Jordan releases and designer pieces from Saint Laurent. He’s also mentioned loving the time he spends organizing his closet and putting together casual outfits.The interest gives him a creative outlet away from his day job as a golfer. He has to stick to the sponsorship and tournament rules with his tournament clothing, but in his personal life he has more freedom to express himself.Thomas is a big college football fan as well, especially the Alabama Crimson Tide. Away from the PGA Tour, his ties to the University of Alabama are still a part of his identity.His houses also reportedly had entertainment areas with multiple televisions and Alabama-themed pool tables. These features are a testament to his love of watching sports and kicking back with friends and family.Thomas' lifestyle also reflects the casual waterfront culture in and around Jupiter. His tastes at the table have been tied to local spots such as Square Grouper Tiki Bar and U-Tiki Beach.They have a relaxed feel that is a nice contrast to the programmed schedules and hospitality packages that accompany major golf tournaments.Fundamentally, Thomas’ Florida home is more than just a luxury property. The waterfront setting, family atmosphere and entertainment facilities provide a personal escape from the professional game of golf. The PGA Tour necessitates consistency, prep, and endless travel, but his non-competitive life offers him family, fashion, football, and the South Florida lifestyle.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.summary: Before the Warriors host the Suns, here's all the info you need for Monday's contest, including how to watch.
articles.body:
The Golden State Warriors have officially hit their first win streak of the 2026-27 campign. After opening the season with three straight losses, the Warriors have rattled off four consecutive wins, including a 124-112 win over the Los Angeles Clippers on Sunday in the first leg of a back-to-back at Chase Center. On Monday, the Warriors will welcome the last team to hand them a loss, the Phoenix Suns . On Oct. 24, the Suns defeated a short-handed edition of the Warriors, 131-122.

Monday's game, the Warriors should be close to full strength. Steph Curry and Draymond Green were sidelined Sunday and are expected to return to the lineup on Monday night. Without Curry and Green, rookie Yaxel Lendeborg tallied a career-high 37 points on the way to a 124-112 win over the Clippers.

articles.title: Warriors get positive update on Stephen Curry ahead of Suns match
articles.summary: It's looking like Stephen Curry will be back on Monday night against the Phoenix Suns.
articles.body:
On Monday night, the Golden State Warriors are slated to finish off their back-to-back matches with a game against the Phoenix Suns . Monday night's affair finds the Warriors in the midst of a four-game win streak, with their most recent triumph coming against the Los Angeles Clippers on Sunday night.

An important factor in their win against the Clippers is that it came without Stephen Curry, who missed the match due to right knee injury management. When he's not on the court, it leaves Steve Kerr and the rest of Golden State's lineup with a 29.2-point hole to make up. But rookie Yaxel Lendeborg led the charge for the Warriors, dropping 37 points and six assists.

However, it doesn't appear that Kerr will need Lendeborg to lead things again, as they're set to regain their leading scorer on Monday night.

As reported by ESPN's Anthony Slater, Curry will be among the players to return to the Warriors' lineup on Monday night, with the other notable name being Draymond Green, who missed out on Sunday's match due to a similar reason as his championship-winning co-star: injury management.

Tip-off between Golden State and Phoenix is slated for 10:00 p.m. EST.
